name: Foxglove
license: Proprietary; the Foxglove SDK (with Foxglove Bridge) and MCAP are MIT. Foxglove Studio 1.x, open source under MPL 2.0, stopped at v1.87.0 in February 2024
summary: An observability platform for robots: a web and desktop app that replays and visualizes multimodal robot data, such as 3D scenes, camera video, plots and maps, on top of a data platform that stores, indexes and searches MCAP recordings.
intro: Robots log many parallel streams at once: cameras, lidar, IMU, plus the output of perception, planning and control. The Foxglove app, in a browser or as a desktop app, lays those streams out in panels (more than 20, including 3D, image, plot, map and state transitions) arranged into layouts a team can share. The same panels work on local files (MCAP, ROS 1 bags, ROS 2 `.db3` files, PX4 ULog) and on live data: Foxglove Bridge streams from a ROS robot, and the open-source Foxglove SDK, a Rust core with Python and C++ bindings, streams from your own code over a local WebSocket while writing the same messages to an MCAP file.

Behind the app sits the Data Platform. Foxlet, which runs on the robot, uploads recordings, which are indexed by device, time and topic. Data Search queries messages, events, devices, recordings and sessions with no separate warehouse, and Events and Sessions mark and group the runs that matter. The data can live in Foxglove’s cloud, in your own S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob bucket (Bring Your Own Storage, indexed in place with read-only access) or in a self-hosted deployment. Remote Access, generally available since August 2026, streams a field robot’s topics over WebRTC through a Foxglove-managed selective forwarding unit, with no VPN, and carries teleoperation commands back.

Pricing is a free tier, Pro from $20 a month with usage billing, and custom Enterprise plans; students and researchers with a `.edu` or `.ac` address get it free. Foxglove started as an open-core project, but with Foxglove 2.0 in March 2024 the company merged its visualization app and data platform into one closed-source product and stopped developing the open-source Foxglove Studio.
strengths: One tool for recorded and live data: the same panels and layouts open MCAP files, ROS bags and live robots, with more than 20 built-in panels for 3D, images, plots and maps
Recordings stay in open formats (MCAP, ROS 1 bags), and Bring Your Own Storage indexes them where they already sit in S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob, without making a copy
Remote Access streams live topics from robots behind firewalls or on cellular links over WebRTC, and the selective forwarding unit gives each viewer its own bitrate
Free for individuals and small teams (10 GB, 3 users, 5 devices); Pro starts at $20 a month with 1 TB and 3 Developer Seats, plus unlimited free Basic Seats for people who only view
limits: Closed source since 2.0: the last open-source Studio release was v1.87.0 in February 2024, so teams that need the source must maintain a community fork of that MPL 2.0 code themselves

Usage billing on several meters (storage, query time, indexing and egress bandwidth) plus $42 a month per extra Developer Seat and $20 per active device, so the bill follows usage; Foxglove offers a cost calculator to estimate it
Key features are tiered: Remote Access needs Pro or Enterprise, self-hosted data needs Enterprise, and the Grafana integration is an Enterprise add-on
Built for robot recordings, not service telemetry: uptime, deploy and cluster dashboards stay in tools like Grafana, and the agent sidebar and Semantic Search launched in beta in August 2026

size_channel.log({"size": size})             # stamped with the current time

story: Adrian Macneil spent years leading infrastructure and developer productivity at the self-driving car company Cruise, where less than half of the engineers worked on the vehicle’s own software. The rest built CI/CD, fleet management, data infrastructure and simulation in-house, and colleagues at other autonomous vehicle and robotics companies were building nearly identical stacks. One of those tools was Webviz, Cruise’s open-source browser app for visualizing ROS data. Macneil and co-founder Roman started Foxglove to sell that kind of tooling off the shelf, beginning with a fork of Webviz released as a desktop app in 2021.

The company raised a $3.7 million seed round led by Amplify Partners (announced January 2022), launched the MCAP log format in February 2022 and raised a $15 million Series A led by Eclipse Ventures that October, by which time its user base had grown more than eight times in a year. It ran two products: Foxglove Studio for visualization, open source, and Foxglove Data Platform for data management, closed source.

In March 2024 Foxglove 2.0 merged the two into one product for web and desktop, introduced new pricing and ended the open-source edition of Studio. Since then the company has released the Foxglove SDK (April 2025), raised a $40 million Series B led by Bessemer Venture Partners (November 2025), cut Pro to $20 a month (April 2026) and, in August 2026, repositioned as an “agentic data platform for physical AI” with an in-app agent, an MCP server, Semantic Search and generally available Remote Access.

choices.why: Leaving the browser sandbox let the first Foxglove connect directly to a ROS 1 stack and escape the browser’s performance limits on large amounts of robot data, while still running on Linux, Windows and macOS.

choices.choice: One product for visualization and data
choices.why: Users said that separate visualization and data management products meant constant context switching and inconsistent web and desktop apps, so 2.0 merged the two codebases.

Visualization took most of the development effort and delivered most of the value to customers, while community contributions were under 1% of commits; the company said it couldn’t sustain full-time development while releasing most of its code as open source.
Foxglove argues that open formats are the only option for storing critical robotics data, so MCAP and the libraries around it stayed open source, and the MIT-licensed SDK writes MCAP files.
